'''Bruce Bernard Smith''' (born June 18, 1963) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[defensive end]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 19 seasons, primarily with the [[Buffalo Bills]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Virginia Tech Hokies football|Virginia Tech Hokies]], earning [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors twice, and was selected by the Bills [[List of first overall NFL draft picks|first overall]] in the [[1985 NFL draft]].

Considered one of the greatest defensive ends of all time, Smith is the [[List of NFL career sacks leaders|NFL's all-time career leader]] in quarterback sacks with 200.{{efn|Note that the NFL only began tracking sacks as an official statistic in 1982, three years before Smith entered the league.}} Smith also received 11 [[Pro Bowl]] selections and eight first-team [[All-Pro]] honors, while appearing in four consecutive [[Super Bowl]]s with the Bills. He was inducted to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2006 and the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2009.

'''Bryan Christopher Barker''' (born June 28, 1964) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Punter (football)|punter]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Santa Clara Broncos football|Santa Clara Broncos]].

Barker last played for the [[St. Louis Rams]] in [[2005 St. Louis Rams season|2005]].  Barker has previously played with the [[Kansas City Chiefs]], [[Philadelphia Eagles]], [[Jacksonville Jaguars]], [[Washington Redskins]], and [[Green Bay Packers]].

On November 28, 2002, during week 13 of the NFL season against the [[Dallas Cowboys]], Barker experienced a severely broken nose, a subdural hematoma, while playing in a nationally televised game.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20210626211027/https://www.espn.com/nfl/recap/_/gameId/221128006 Redskins vs Cowboys - Game Recap - November 28, 2002 - ESPN]</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Maske | first=Mark | title=Punter's Famous Feat Was a Knee to Nose | website=The Washington Post | date=2003-08-14 | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/2003/08/14/punters-famous-feat-was-a-knee-to-nose/dd2a4312-4d05-4158-9b00-a90f3663b181/ | access-date=2025-10-21}}</ref>

[[Aaron Schatz]] of statistics site [[Football Outsiders]] noted a punt Barker kicked "in 1999 that was just ridiculous, far past any baseline I had ever created. In Week 5, on the road against the [[New York Jets|Jets]], [Barker] punted the ball from the Jaguars' own 5-yard line to the Jets' 12-yard line, an 83-yard punt <ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.footballoutsiders.com/dvoa-ratings/2005/1999-dvoa-ratings-and-commentary |title=1999 DVOA Ratings and Commentary |access-date=2011-06-07 |archive-date=2017-08-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170816110655/http://www.footballoutsiders.com/dvoa-ratings/2005/1999-dvoa-ratings-and-commentary |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Highly versatile, Matthews played every position on the offensive line throughout his NFL career, starting in 99 games as a [[left guard]], 87 as a center, 67 as a [[right guard]], 22 as a [[right tackle]], 17 as a [[left tackle]], and was the [[long snapper]] on field goals, extra points, and punts. Matthews played [[college football]] for the [[USC Trojans football|USC Trojans]], where he was recognized as a consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] as a senior. Matthews was selected in the first round (ninth overall) of the [[1983 NFL draft]] by the [[Houston Oilers]] and was a 14-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection, tied for the second-most in NFL history, in addition to a nine-time first-team [[All-Pro]]. Matthews was inducted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2007, and his number 74 jersey is [[Retired number|retired]] by the Titans. After retiring as a player, Matthews served as an assistant coach for the [[Houston Texans]] and Titans. A member of the [[Matthews family]] of football players, he is the brother of linebacker [[Clay Matthews Jr.]]; father of center [[Kevin Matthews (American football)|Kevin Matthews]] and tackle [[Jake Matthews (American football)|Jake Matthews]]; and uncle of linebacker [[Clay Matthews III]] and linebacker [[Casey Matthews]].

'''Bruce Alan Hardy''' (born June 1, 1956, in [[Murray, Utah]]), is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[tight end]] for the [[Miami Dolphins]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Arizona State Sun Devils football|Arizona State Sun Devils]] and was selected by the Dolphins in the ninth round of the [[1978 NFL draft]]. Hardy played his entire NFL career with the Dolphins from 1978 to 1989. He was married to Joanie Hardy for 20 years and has four sons: Nathan,<ref>[http://www.nathanhardy.com nathan hardy | interactive portfolio<!-- Bot generated title -->]  {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071009044317/http://www.nathanhardy.com/ |date=October 9, 2007 }}</ref> Adam, Aaron and Matthew. He [[Coach (sport)|coached]] in the [[Arena Football League (1987–2008)|Arena Football League]] for the [[Florida Bobcats]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.arenafan.com/history/?page=coaches&coach=47|title=Bruce Hardy - AFL Coaches - ArenaFan.com|website=www.arenafan.com}}</ref> before coaching for [[Florida International University]].

In 1974, while in high school, Hardy appeared on the cover of [[Sports Illustrated]].<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://sicovers.com/featured/bingham-high-school-qb-bruce-hardy-april-29-1974-sports-illustrated-cover.html |title=High School's Bruce Hardy |website=Sports Illustrated Covers |date=April 29, 1974 |access-date=December 20, 2021}}</ref> He was the 4th prep player so honored, but the first football player.  The first three being all high school basketball stars.

'''Bruce Alan Wilkerson''' (born July 28, 1964) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] for three [[National Football League]] (NFL) teams from 1987 to 1997. He started in [[Super Bowl XXXI]] for the [[Green Bay Packers]].  Wilkerson played [[college football]] for the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]], twice earning [[List of All-SEC football teams|All-SEC]] honors.

Wilkerson attended Loudon High School in [[Loudon, Tennessee]], where he played both offensive tackle and defensive tackle, and was named to the all-state team his senior year.<ref>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=742&pg=64 1982 Tennessee Signees] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304061447/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=742&pg=64 |date=March 4, 2016 }}," ''1982 Tennessee Volunteers Football Guide'' (University of Tennessee, 1982), p. 62.</ref>  He signed with Tennessee in 1982, though he was a [[redshirt (college sports)|redshirt]] his first year.

Working with Tennessee offensive line coach (and future head coach) [[Phillip Fulmer]], Wilkerson secured a spot in the second string during the 1983 season, backing up veteran tackle Curt Singer.<ref>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=198&pg=56 1983 Squad] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304084104/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=198&pg=56 |date=March 4, 2016 }}," ''1983 Tennessee Volunteers Football Program'' (University of Tennessee, 1983), p. 59.</ref>  By his sophomore season in 1984, he was a starter, anchoring a line that helped running back [[Johnnie Jones]] set career rushing records.<ref>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=738&pg=77 1985 Squad] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304084109/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=738&pg=77 |date=March 4, 2016 }}," ''1985 Tennessee Volunteers Football Program'' (University of Tennessee, 1985), pp. 74, 112-113.</ref>  Wilkerson was an integral member of the [[1985 Tennessee Volunteers football team|1985 "Sugar Vols" squad]], and was named All-SEC and 2nd-team All-American at the end of the season.<ref>"[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=748&pg=80 1986 Squad] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131219133138/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=748&pg=80 |date=December 19, 2013 }}," ''1986 Tennessee Volunteers Football Guide'' (University of Tennessee, 1986), p. 79.</ref>  In the [[1986 Sugar Bowl]], Wilkerson's block on [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami]] nose guard [[Jerome Brown]] helped spring [[Jeff Powell (American football)|Jeff Powell]]'s 60-yard touchdown run.<ref>Keith Jackson and Frank Broyles, game commentary, 1986 Sugar Bowl television broadcast, ABC Sports, January 1, 1986.</ref>

After an All-SEC senior year in 1986, Wilkerson was selected by the [[Los Angeles Raiders]] in the second round of the [[1987 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1987 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1987/draft.htm |access-date=2023-09-25 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  He spent his first eight seasons with the Raiders, and was a starter throughout the early 1990s.  He was on the inaugural roster of the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] in 1995, and closed out his career with Green Bay.

'''Bruce Kozerski''' (born April 2, 1962) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Center (American football)|center]] for 12 seasons with the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).<ref name=lloyd/> He played [[college football]] for the [[Holy Cross Crusaders football|Holy Cross Crusaders]].

He graduated from [[James M. Coughlin High School]] in [[Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania]].<ref name=lloyd>{{cite web|first=Steve|last=Lloyd|url=http://wnep.com/2012/03/22/former-nfl-lineman-bruce-kozerski-visits-misericordia-university-5/|title=Former NFL Lineman Bruce Kozerski Visits Misericordia University|date=22 March 2012 |publisher=WNEP News}}</ref> He graduated from the [[College of the Holy Cross]] in Worcester, MA with a major in Physics and later acquired a Master's in teaching from Xavier University. He was an alternate in the 1988, 1989, and 1990 Pro Bowls. "Mr. Versatile", as he was called, retired after the 1995 season. He is a teacher at [[Holy Cross High School (Covington, Kentucky)|Holy Cross High School]] in [[Covington, Kentucky]] where he teaches physics, pre-calculus, and calculus. He is also the head football coach at Holy Cross as well. He lives in [[Edgewood, Kentucky]].

On November 25, 2011, Kozerski, in his eighth year as head coach, led Holy Cross High School's Covington football team to the Kentucky High School Athletic Association Division 2A, state football championship. It was the Indians' first appearance in the state championship game. Holy Cross defeated Glasgow High School 33–14 in the championship game.

Kozerski was inducted into the Kentucky Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2017.

'''Bruce Daniel Scholtz''' (born September 26, 1958) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for seven seasons with the [[Seattle Seahawks]] and one season with the [[New England Patriots]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas Longhorns]].

Scholtz attended [[David Crockett High School (Austin, Texas)|David Crockett High School]] in [[Austin, Texas]]. During his senior year, he was a captain of the [[Varsity team|varsity]] football team and played as both linebacker and center. He won the [[Central Texas]] 26AAAA Defensive Player of the Year award. Scholtz also played on the varsity [[basketball]] team. He averaged 19 points per game and led the team in [[Rebound (basketball)|rebounding]].<ref>Crockett Publications. ''Texan '77''. Taylor Publishing Company, 1977.</ref> He graduated from Crockett in 1977 and the [[University of Texas at Austin]] where he played in 22 games over two seasons.

At Texas he was a force on defense, and left the school ranked in the top ten in fumbles recovered, tackles for a loss in a season, career tackles for a loss and total tackles.<ref>{{cite web |title=History of Longhorn Sports |url=https://www.texaslsn.org/top-longhorn-linebackers |access-date=18 January 2024}}</ref>

He was selected in 1982, round 2, pick 6 (33 overall) by the Seattle Seahawks.
